title: Indexes, query plans and tracking cost
summary: Read a query plan, add the index it needs, and stop paying for tracking you do not use.

steps.title: Is my query using an index?
body: Every database can tell you **how** it will run a query: its **query plan**. In SQLite, prefix the SQL with `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`:
```text
EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN SELECT * FROM "Members" WHERE "Email" = 'ana@example.com'
SCAN Members                                                   -- no index: read every row
SEARCH Members USING INDEX IX_Members_Email (Email=?)          -- with one: jump to the row

`SCAN` means a full table scan: fine for 50 rows, terrible for 5 million. `SEARCH ... USING INDEX` means the index narrowed it down. (SQL Server shows the same idea as *Table Scan* against *Index Seek*; PostgreSQL as *Seq Scan* against *Index Scan*.)
The examples in this lesson use a small helper, `Plan(db, sql)`, that runs `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` for a query's SQL (from `ToQueryString()`) and returns the plan's text.

protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=club.db");
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder model) => model.Entity<Member>().HasIndex(m => m.Email).IsUnique();
steps.explain: `Email` has an index, so SQLite searches it. `City` has none, so every row is scanned. (`m` is the alias EF Core gave the table in its SQL.)

steps.title: Which indexes?
body: Index the columns your important queries **filter, join or sort** on:
- **Foreign keys** are indexed automatically by EF Core (`IX_Books_AuthorId`), because joins and `Include` use them.
- **Lookups by a natural value** (email, SKU, slug): a unique index.
- **Filter plus sort**: a composite index in that order, e.g. `(City, Age)` serves `WHERE City = @c ORDER BY Age`.
And what an index cannot help:
- a function on the column: `WHERE lower(Email) = ...` cannot use an index on `Email` (store a normalised copy, or use a case-insensitive collation),
- a leading wildcard: `LIKE '%son'`,
- a low-selectivity column on its own (a `bool` that is true for half the rows).
Every index slows writes and takes space, so add them for real queries you have measured, not "just in case".

code: static string Plan(DbContext db, string sql)
// ToQueryString starts with ".param set" lines when the query has parameters: they are not SQL.
protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=club.db");
protected override void OnModelCreating(ModelBuilder model) => model.Entity<Member>().HasIndex(m => new { m.City, m.Age });
steps.explain: The composite index starts with `City`, so the first query searches it, and the rows come out already sorted by `Age` (no extra sort step). The second filters only on `Age`, the index's second column, so it cannot seek and scans the table.

steps.title: The cost of tracking
body: Tracking queries do real work per entity: build it, look it up in the identity map (so the same row is always the same object), store a snapshot of its values, and compare snapshots in every `SaveChanges`.
For read-only work, skip it:
- `AsNoTracking()`: no snapshots, no identity map. If the same author appears on 100 books, you get 100 separate `Author` objects.
- `AsNoTrackingWithIdentityResolution()`: no tracking, but duplicates are still merged into one object.
- A projection (`Select`): nothing to track at all.
And keep contexts **short-lived**. A context that has loaded 100,000 entities makes every later `SaveChanges` slower, because it must check them all.

protected override void OnConfiguring(DbContextOptionsBuilder options) => options.UseSqlite("Data Source=library.db")

An index is sorted by the column's value, so equality, prefixes and ordering can use it. A function of the column or a suffix match needs every value examined.

steps.title: Make it seek
prompt: The members screen runs this query all day:
db.Members.Where(m => m.City == city && m.Age >= minAge).OrderBy(m => m.Age)

Write the `ClubDb` context (`Data Source=club.db`, `DbSet<Member> Members`) with an index that lets SQLite **search** (not scan) for it, and also a **unique** index on `Email`. The tests give you `Member` (`Id`, `Email`, `City`, `Age`) and check the query plans.
